seoTitle: Extract Data From a PDF to Google Sheets Easily
metaDescription: Pull tables out of a PDF into Google Sheets with a Workspace Marketplace add-on: install it from Extensions, pick the pages, process them, then clean up the result. Plus what to do with scanned PDFs.
intro:
Retyping figures from an invoice or report is slow, and one wrong keystroke becomes a bad total three tabs later. Google Sheets can't open a PDF and read its tables by itself. Add-ons from the Google Workspace Marketplace fill that gap, and once one is installed the job is mostly point and click.

This guide installs an extraction add-on from inside Sheets, runs it against a sample PDF, and covers the cleanup that almost every extraction needs. The add-on in the walkthrough opens a dialog titled PDF to Sheets. Others in the Marketplace work along similar lines, but their buttons, free limits and OCR support differ, so read the listing before you install.
costNote: Google doesn't charge for add-ons, but the developers set their own pricing, and many PDF extractors cap the free tier by page count. One Marketplace listing from a developer named PDF to Sheets, for example, allows 5 free pages before a paid plan. Check the Pricing line on a listing before you rely on it for a long document.

steps.heading: Install a PDF extraction add-on
steps.body:
Open a spreadsheet and click Extensions > Add-ons > Get add-ons. The Google Workspace Marketplace opens on top of the sheet, already filtered to apps that work with Sheets, and each card shows a rating and install count. Search "pdf" and pick a tool that says it converts PDF tables to Sheets. A general document utility won't do the same job.

Click the add-on to read its full description, then click Install and Continue. Most add-ons ask for access to data they need, such as the spreadsheet they'll write into. Read the request, click Allow, then Done.

image.caption: The Google Workspace Marketplace opened from inside Sheets, filtered to apps that work with Sheets, each card showing its rating and install count.

steps.heading: Launch it from the Extensions menu
steps.body:
Installed add-ons don't get a menu of their own. They sit under Extensions, each with a submenu for opening it.

Before launching, decide where the data should land. A blank tab keeps the import away from anything you've already built, and it's easier to spot a misaligned column against an empty grid.

image.caption: A spreadsheet with the pointer on the Extensions menu, where installed add-ons are launched.

steps.heading: Pick the pages and process them
steps.body:
After you upload the PDF, the PDF to Sheets dialog shows every page as a numbered thumbnail. Click a page to select it and it highlights in blue. Hold Shift to select a run of consecutive pages. There are also Select All and Clear buttons.

Select only the pages that hold tables. Cover pages and running text add rows you'll just delete later, and on a page-capped free tier they use up your allowance. Then click Process Selected Pages and the add-on writes what it finds into the spreadsheet.

image.caption: The PDF to Sheets dialog with a page-by-page preview, plus Select All, Clear and Process Selected Pages buttons.

steps.heading: Check and clean up the output
steps.body:
Clean tables with clear rows and columns usually come through intact. Merged cells, entries that wrap onto two lines, and uneven spacing are where things go wrong.

Scroll through before you build anything on top. Look for three things. Numbers stored as text sit left-aligned instead of right-aligned, and SUM ignores them. Dates may arrive in an unexpected format. Columns can split or merge if the PDF's layout wasn't a strict grid. For text that landed in one cell but belongs in several, use Data > Split text to columns. Then set number and date formats explicitly from the Format menu instead of trusting Sheets' guess. If you pull the same kind of document every month, keep the destination tab's columns the same each time so the checks become routine.

troubleshooting.problem: The add-on returns nothing, or gibberish, for a scanned PDF
troubleshooting.cause: A scanned page is an image with no text layer, so a tool without OCR has nothing to read.
troubleshooting.fix: Use an add-on whose listing mentions OCR for scanned PDFs. For plain text (not tables), Google Drive's own Open with > Google Docs converts PDFs of 2 MB or smaller, though Google warns tables are not likely to be detected.

troubleshooting.problem: The add-on no longer appears under Extensions
troubleshooting.cause: It has been turned off for this spreadsheet.
troubleshooting.fix: Go to Extensions > Add-ons > Manage add-ons, open the add-on's Options (three dots) and turn on Use in this document.

troubleshooting.problem: Totals don't add up after import
troubleshooting.cause: Some numbers came in as text, often because of currency symbols, stray spaces or thousands separators in the PDF.
troubleshooting.fix: Select the column and apply Format > Number. Any cells still left-aligned need their stray characters removed first.

faq.question: Can Google Sheets read a PDF without an add-on?
faq.answer: No. Sheets has no built-in PDF import. You need a Marketplace add-on, or you can convert the PDF to text in Google Drive first and paste it across, which loses the table structure.

faq.question: What about scanned PDFs?
faq.answer: A scanned PDF is really an image, so it needs OCR. Some add-ons include it. Google Drive can also OCR a PDF via Open with > Google Docs, but only files of 2 MB or less, and Google says tables are not likely to survive.

faq.question: Can I extract only certain pages of a long PDF?
faq.answer: Yes, in the add-on shown here. Click individual thumbnails, or hold Shift to select a consecutive range, then click Process Selected Pages.

faq.question: How do I remove an add-on I no longer want?
faq.answer: Open Extensions > Add-ons > Manage add-ons, click Options next to the add-on, and choose Uninstall.
